what: On Earth page (#/earth): three cards, each linking a finding already on this site to an Earth use. The wording is the team's. No number is typed in this file: every number is a {ref:{file, path}} item that the page reads from data/<file>.json at run time, and a card with no ref shows no number. Path grammar: dot-separated keys; [n] picks array item n; [key=value,key2=value2] picks the first array item whose fields equal those values. fmt: num (d digits), sig, pct (a 0-1 share shown as a percentage), count (length of an array), text (a quoted string from the file); map turns a stored code into words.

units.note: Each ref carries its own unit, copied from the units block of the file it reads (flex_suppression: burns; smoke_sizes: nm and share of smoke mass; flame_spread: O2 as a 0-1 mole fraction, kPa, m/s, mm/s; spread_predictor: mm/s, cm/s, vol%).

text.h: What it could mean on Earth

text.t: Water mist is one of the responses the challenge brief names. Mist and added gases both change what surrounds a flame, and FLEX shows that what surrounds a droplet flame decides whether it goes out. That is a reason to judge mist by what sensors measure on the flame, not by eye. Our bench rig runs at Earth gravity, so a completed mist trial would be an Earth result, not a space result.
FLEX added gases around fuel droplets; it did not spray water. No test on this site shows mist putting out a fire, on Earth or in orbit.

text.h: What it could mean on Earth

text.t: Light-scattering smoke detectors are used on Earth too. The SAME results are a reason to ask how a detector responds to very fine smoke from specific materials, and not only to smoke in general.
This is smoke made in microgravity from a handful of spacecraft materials. No Earth detector was tested, and nothing here says that smoke detectors fail in general. The detector limit is a choice (

text.h: What it could mean on Earth

text.t: Flame-spread tests on Earth run with gravity pulling hot gas upward. These models show that airflow, oxygen and gravity, not only the material, decide whether a flame spreads and how fast. That is a reason to test materials, including fabrics for protective gear, across the airflow and oxygen levels they will meet, not at one standard condition.

No firefighter gear was tested. The fabric is one NASA sample material, and the acrylic numbers come from a physics model checked against NASA's BASS-II flights, not from a burn on Earth. Nothing here rates a material or a piece of gear for use.
